brief.head: Stone Age hardware
brief.text: Modern hu­mans have had only about 4,000 gen­er­a­tions, Ajay Shah said, too few to change the brain’s hard­ware. Many fal­la­cies are in­stincts that once worked and now mis­fire. {045-C01}

brief.head: Three ways to disagree
brief.text: We fight over facts, over val­ues or over how we rea­son, Shah said. He hopes logic, ar­gu­ment and proof can be com­mon ground. {045-C02}

brief.head: A gift that grows
brief.text: Newton, the Magna Carta and the tran­sis­tor were each made in some cor­ner of the world, and ev­ery­one came out bet­ter off. {045-C04}

brief.head: Varma’s Law
brief.text: Amit Varma, being “a lit­tle vain”, named a law after him­self: most in­ter­fer­ence in free mar­kets re­dis­tributes from the poor to the rich. {045-C05}

brief.head: Not a company
brief.text: A coun­try is not a firm, Shah said: a state’s every move rip­ples through the whole econ­omy, and it wields co­er­cion. {045-C08}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why we keep fighting
lead.head: Five traps for Stone Age brains

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma at the start of Episode 45

body: The two hosts could not agree on who should speak first. Amit Varma turned the fum­ble into the ques­tion of the hour: why do we keep fight­ing? {045-J01}

Their an­swer, over the next 55 min­utes, was that our brains are wired for a world that no longer ex­ists. The world is too com­plex to grasp, so we make sense of it through sim­ple sto­ries. Those sto­ries clash with one an­other, and some­times all of them clash with re­al­ity.

“From a hun­dred thou­sand years ago to today, the pe­riod of mod­ern man is a mere 4,000 gen­er­a­tions,” Ajay Shah said, “which is not enough to ma­te­ri­ally move the nee­dle on our hard­ware.” {045-C01}

Taking their frame­work from Thomas Sowell’s *Economic Facts and Fallacies*, the hosts walked through five fal­la­cies that grow out of in­stincts formed in small tribes of hunter-gatherers. Each once served the tribe well. Each mis­fires in a mod­ern econ­omy. {045-R01}
## The five traps
The zero-sum fal­lacy treats the econ­omy as a fixed pie, so that one person’s gain must be another’s loss. {045-C03}
The fal­lacy of com­po­si­tion as­sumes that what is true of a part is true of the whole. {045-C06}
The post-hoc fal­lacy de­cides that be­cause one thing fol­lowed an­other, the first must have caused the sec­ond. {045-C09}
The chess-pieces fal­lacy imag­ines so­ci­ety as a board that a plan­ner can ar­range. {045-C12}
The open-ended fal­lacy for­gets that re­sources are lim­ited and have other uses. {045-C13}
The ex­am­ples ran from a col­lege hos­tel in Pune to the banks of the Nile and a mon­key throw­ing darts.
## Why it mat­ters

For the hosts the stakes are prac­ti­cal. Zero-sum think­ing, Varma ar­gued, drives statism and the con­fu­sion of in­equal­ity with poverty. Since 1991, hun­dreds of mil­lions of Indians have left poverty even as in­equal­ity rose.
“In a world of dou­ble thank you mo­ments,” Varma said, “the only way that I can profit is by mak­ing you bet­ter off.” {045-C03}

The fal­lacy of com­po­si­tion, Shah said, is the core dif­fer­ence be­tween think­ing like a firm and think­ing about an econ­omy. What makes sense for one ex­porter, or one tomato farmer, can wreck things when ev­ery­one does it, and worse when the state uses its power to make ev­ery­one do it. {045-C06}

Millions of Indians, Varma said, stayed poor for longer than they should have, be­cause plan­ners did not trust people’s in­ge­nu­ity. Shah was less sure that the les­son had been learnt. “Gentle read­ers,” he said, “see how op­ti­mistic Amit is.” {045-J11}
## How to stop fight­ing

Knowing these fal­la­cies is easy, Shah warned; in­ter­nal­is­ing them takes a long time. In a doc­tor, en­gi­neer and MBA India that treats knowl­edge as a trade to be ap­plied, he said, “there is a great cri­sis of think­ing”. {045-C18}

Both hosts ended with books about the fight­ing it­self. Shah rec­om­mended Christopher Blattman’s *Why We Fight*, glad that an econ­o­mist had “opened the box of vi­o­lence”. {045-R24} Varma chose Arnold Kling’s *The Three Languages of Politics*, which ar­gues that po­lit­i­cal tribes talk past each other be­cause they start from dif­fer­ent core val­ues: equal­ity, tra­di­tion or free­dom. {045-R25}
Recognising the other person’s first prin­ci­ple, Varma said, is also a way of recog­nis­ing their hu­man­ity. {045-C17}
And if the fight­ing never quite stops? Varma reached for an old motto: “Pessimism of the in­tel­lect, op­ti­mism of the will.” {045-J18}

second.label: The Great Depression
second.head: The crash didn’t do it
second.deck: Amit Varma, drawing on Thomas Sowell, blames what came after 1929

pic.caption: Unemployed men queue outside a soup kitchen in Chicago, February 1931

body: The stan­dard story is that the stock mar­ket crash of 1929 caused the Great Depression. Amit Varma, draw­ing on Thomas Sowell, told a dif­fer­ent one. {045-S04}

In the months after the crash, un­em­ploy­ment peaked at about 9 per cent, and by June 1930 it was down to around 6.5 per cent. {#unemployment} Then the gov­ern­ment began to in­ter­vene, first with the Smoot-Hawley tar­iff and then with a se­ries of other mea­sures. That is when things ex­ploded.

Sowell also points to a later stock mar­ket crash that was fol­lowed by decades of strong growth. Varma added that Amity Shlaes’s *The Forgotten Man*, if he re­mem­bered cor­rectly, makes a sim­i­lar case. {045-R10}

quote.text: It wasn’t the stock mar­ket crash. It was a whole bunch of in­ter­ven­tions which led to the prob­lem.

third.head: Nile floods, coat blamed

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the witch doctor’s coat

body: A witch doc­tor claims that every spring he takes off his coat, and then the Nile floods, so the river must be an­swer­ing his coat. The se­quence is real, Ajay Shah said. The causal claim is ab­surd. {045-S02}
Press a but­ton and get a bis­cuit a sec­ond later, and two or three tries will con­vince you that you caused it. Make it ten hours, and the mind can no longer con­nect the two. {045-C10}
Our sense of cause and ef­fect, Shah ar­gued, was built for a world of tigers and deer, where ef­fects fol­low causes quickly. So we must lean on ev­i­dence and data rather than gut feel.
Amit Varma, who is on a keto diet, did not want the bis­cuit at all. “Bacon strips,” he said, “an­other mat­ter.” {045-J06}

p2.title: The five fallacies
p2.deck: From Thomas Sowell’s *Economic Facts and Fallacies*, as argued over by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

from1.head: Five traps for Stone Age brains

quote.text: In a world of dou­ble thank you mo­ments, the only way that I can profit is by mak­ing you bet­ter off.

photo.caption: Thomas Sowell in 1964. His book set the episode’s agenda

box.title: The book behind the episode
box.text: *Economic Facts and Fallacies* names fal­la­cies that are foun­da­tional, in that many other er­rors grow out of them. Sowell is one of Amit Varma’s in­tel­lec­tual he­roes, “still going strong at ninety plus”. {045-R01}

sections.label: Fallacy One
sections.head: Thank you. No, thank you
sections.caption: the zero-sum fallacy
body: When a tribe splits a deer, every chunk one hunter takes is a chunk an­other can­not have. Our in­stincts were formed in that world, Amit Varma said, which is why we so read­ily see the econ­omy as a fixed pie. {045-C03}

Modern ex­change is dif­fer­ent. When you buy a cof­fee, you say thank you and the seller says thank you, be­cause both of you are bet­ter off. Varma took the image from the colum­nist John Stossel, who calls it the dou­ble thank-you mo­ment. {045-R02}

Treat the world as a fixed pie and re­dis­tri­bu­tion looks like the an­swer. But re­dis­tri­bu­tion al­ways trades off against growth, Varma said, and what a poor coun­try needs is growth. Since 1991, hun­dreds of mil­lions of Indians have left poverty even as in­equal­ity rose.
## The great­est pos­i­tive-sum game

Ajay Shah took the ar­gu­ment fur­ther. Newton, the Magna Carta and the tran­sis­tor were each cre­ated in some cor­ner of the world, and ev­ery­one came out bet­ter off: the in­ven­tors of the tran­sis­tor did not gain at our ex­pense. Knowledge, he said, is “the great­est pos­i­tive sum game story of the world”. {045-C04}

In per­sonal life, Varma ar­gued against crabby scarcity think­ing and for gen­eros­ity, be­cause some­one else’s suc­cess is not your loss. Shah’s book for the oc­ca­sion was Robert Axelrod’s *The Evolution of Cooperation*, which works out the best re­sponse to being wronged: strike back once, but not twice, not thrice, not for­ever. {045-R06}

quote.text: In a world of dou­ble thank you mo­ments, the only way that I can profit is by mak­ing you bet­ter off.

sections.label: Fallacy Two
sections.head: When everyone stands up
sections.caption: the fallacy of composition
body: Amit Varma read out Thomas Sowell’s il­lus­tra­tion: “A base­ball fan at a ball­park can see the game bet­ter by stand­ing up. But if all the fans stand up, they will not all see bet­ter.” {045-C06}

This is the fal­lacy of com­po­si­tion, the be­lief that what is true of a part is true of the whole. Politicians help one group and present its gains as gains for so­ci­ety, which is re­ally rob­bing Peter to pay Paul.

Ajay Shah sees it as the core dif­fer­ence be­tween think­ing like a firm and think­ing about an econ­omy. Exporting more makes sense for one com­pany. Using state power to sub­sidise land, elec­tric­ity or the ex­change rate so that every com­pany ex­ports can un­bal­ance the econ­omy. The test, he said, is al­ways the same: what if ev­ery­one does it?
## The flip side

Varma turned the fal­lacy in­side out. Stereotyping takes a trait seen in one mem­ber of a group and paints every mem­ber with it. One so­cio­pathic econ­o­mist does not make all econ­o­mists so­ciopaths, he said, as­sur­ing Shah that he was not one of them. {045-J07}
People regress to the mean, he said: nei­ther an­gels nor demons. He read out a line from Tim Urban to the same ef­fect: “Angels and demons aren’t real.” {045-R07}

quote.text: We are all human, we are all frail, and we are all beau­ti­ful.

sections.label: Fallacy Three
sections.head: Wet streets don’t cause rain
sections.caption: the post-hoc fallacy
body: Something hap­pened, and then some­thing else hap­pened, so the first thing must have caused the sec­ond. That, Amit Varma said, is the post-hoc fal­lacy: *post hoc ergo propter hoc*. {045-C09}

Its cousin, *cum hoc ergo propter hoc*, as­sumes that two things hap­pen­ing to­gether must be causally linked. And Michael Crichton’s phrase, “wet streets cause rain”, cap­tures the arrow point­ing the wrong way. {045-R09}

These short­cuts made sense in a sim­ple world, where a rus­tle in the bush meant a tiger. Varma ar­gued that re­li­gion and rit­ual grew out of such sim­ple causal sto­ries, for ex­am­ple about what brings rain. In a com­plex world they mis­lead us con­stantly, es­pe­cially in eco­nom­ics.
## A short-range radar

Ajay Shah of­fered a thought ex­per­i­ment. Press a but­ton and get a bis­cuit one sec­ond later, and you see the cause at once. Make the delay ten hours and you are lost. “The human mind is con­gen­i­tally un­able to see cause and ef­fect play­ing out across longer timescales,” he said. {045-C10}

The per­sonal les­son, for Varma, was hu­mil­ity about the sto­ries we tell about our­selves. Shah’s ver­sion for firms: com­pare your re­sults with sim­ply hold­ing your industry’s shares. Only the out­per­for­mance is yours. {045-C11}

quote.text: 98% of what hap­pens to each of us is sheer dumb luck.

sections.label: Fallacy Four
sections.head: People are not pawns
sections.caption: the chess-pieces fallacy
body: Adam Smith warned of the “man of sys­tem”, who imag­ines he can ar­range the mem­bers of a great so­ci­ety as eas­ily as a hand ar­ranges the pieces on a chess­board. Friedrich Hayek called the same be­lief the fatal con­ceit. {045-R12}

Top-down con­trol works for a tribe, or a fam­ily firm of ten peo­ple, Amit Varma said. At scale, no­body has the in­for­ma­tion. Order emerges in­stead through “human ac­tion, but not human de­sign”, in Adam Ferguson’s phrase. {045-J15}

Ajay Shah traced the idea “all the way to self­ish gene”: every or­gan­ism op­ti­mises for it­self, so no­body can sup­press each person’s drive to pur­sue their own life. He could not re­sist rec­om­mend­ing a Leonard Cohen poem in which a slave says that any sys­tem you de­sign with­out us will not work. {045-R18}
For in­di­vid­u­als, Varma said, the les­son is to focus on pro­cesses and habits, not grand goals.

quote.text: The truth is we are not pieces on a chess­board that you can make things go the way they want.

sections.label: Fallacy Five
sections.head: There is no free lunch
sections.caption: the open-ended fallacy
body: Health, safety and open space are open-ended de­sires. Who could be against them? But re­sources are lim­ited and have other uses, Amit Varma said, quot­ing Thomas Sowell. {045-C13}
India’s big­gest re­li­gion, he said, is gov­ern­ment. We as­sume that *mai-baap sarkar*, the par­ent-government, will pay for ev­ery­thing, as if money were un­lim­ited and cost noth­ing. {045-J14}

Ajay Shah in­voked Milton Friedman: there is no free lunch. Every gov­ern­ment rupee is ex­tracted through tax­a­tion, which is co­er­cive and costly. A re­spon­si­ble pol­icy thinker, he said, should pair every pro­posal for more spend­ing with match­ing cuts else­where. {045-J16}
## The expert’s test

Shah of­fered a con­trar­ian test of ex­per­tise in health. The Indian gov­ern­ment spends poorly, and pre­ven­tion is bet­ter than cure, so the so­phis­ti­cated ex­pert asks for less gov­ern­ment spend­ing on health­care, and more on pub­lic health. {045-C14}

Coercion is worse than spend­ing, he ar­gued, be­cause it has no bud­get. “In spend­ing, there is a bud­get con­straint,” he said. “But un­for­tu­nately, when it gets to co­er­cion, co­er­cion can be lim­it­less.” {045-C15}
## Your own open-ended fal­lacy

For Varma, with age, the bind­ing con­straint has shifted from money to time. He cited Steve Jobs’s ad­vice to his de­signer Jonathan Ive: learn to say no to things that you love. This is not a pro­duc­tiv­ity fetish, he added. Time to relax and chill out is use­ful too. {045-C16}

quote.text: Many de­sir­able things are ad­vo­cated with­out re­gard to the most fun­da­men­tal fact of eco­nom­ics, that re­sources are in­her­ently lim­ited and have al­ter­na­tive uses.
quote.who: Thomas Sowell, as read by Amit Varma

quote.text: One way to get past the fight­ing that we do, this ide­o­log­i­cal bick­er­ing that has be­come so com­mon, is to rec­og­nize the other person’s core first prin­ci­ple, which is also to rec­og­nize that other person’s hu­man­ity.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: The ones you would retell over coffee, and what each one teaches

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s college story, and a fallacy told for laughs
stories.head: The penance that built a Greek god
body: In the late 1980s and early 1990s, Amit Varma was a stu­dent at Ferguson College in Pune, so thin you could count the bones on his ribs. Fresh from a boys’ school, in an arts class that was about 80 per cent girls, he chose be­tween the can­teen and the tapri by the di­rec­tion of the wind, so that his shirt would not blow against his ribs. Gyms were not yet part of the cul­ture.
His con­so­la­tion was Ryan, a de­vout Christian who was just as thin. If the two of them passed a group of girls who gig­gled, Varma could at least hope the gig­gling was at Ryan.

Then one day, through the open door of Ryan’s hos­tel room, Varma saw a hor­ri­fy­ing sight. Ryan was doing push-ups. Thin boys whose bones are vis­i­ble, Varma ex­plained, do not do push-ups. {045-J03}
Ryan ex­plained. Masturbation was a sin, and he had set him­self 25 push-ups as the penance for each time. {#pushups} Varma, in his mind, did *sashtang pranam* and left.
Six months later Ryan was buff. The girls now gig­gled “at the im­prob­a­ble pres­ence of a Greek god in their midst”, and Varma was the only one left whose bones were vis­i­ble. {045-J04}
Then an­other friend from the hos­tel, whom Varma calls Varun, qui­etly asked how to get a body like Ryan’s. Varma told him, de­lib­er­ately and as a joke: you have to mas­tur­bate.
“The les­son here,” Varma said, “is that de­lib­er­ately out of a sense of humor, I com­mit­ted a fal­lacy called the post hoc ergo propter hoc.” {045-S01}
stories.why: One thing hap­pened, then an­other, so the first must have caused the sec­ond. The joke works be­cause the real cause, the push-ups, was hid­den in­side the se­quence. Many of our causal sto­ries leave out the hid­den mid­dle step in the same way.
stories.postscript: Varma, now on keto and one meal a day, says he wants to be like Ryan. Which Ryan? “Any of the two.” {045-J06}

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on luck, Infosys and the CEO
stories.head: The monkey beats the market
body: In fi­nance, it is well ac­cepted that a mon­key throw­ing darts builds a de­cent port­fo­lio, and that nearly all the clever hu­mans pick­ing stocks un­der­per­form it. Hope, though, springs eter­nal. “We each of us think that I’m in that 0.01% of the cool peo­ple that know what to do,” Ajay Shah said. {045-J10}
Nobody could have pre­dicted the soft­ware boom from the mid-1990s. When Infosys went pub­lic in 1994, its IPO was mostly un­der­sub­scribed. {#ipo}

People in­side a boom­ing in­dus­try then credit their suc­cess to their own de­ci­sions. Shah’s hon­est test: how would you have done if you had sim­ply bought shares in ten com­pa­nies in your in­dus­try and done noth­ing? Only the out­per­for­mance over that base­line is yours.
“The world, the so­ci­ety at­tributes all firm suc­cess to the CEO,” he said, “and I think that is wrong.” {045-S06}
stories.why: Much of what passes for suc­cess is the luck of being in soft­ware rather than seafood. Separate the tail­wind from your own con­tri­bu­tion be­fore cred­it­ing the CEO, or your­self.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the dart-throwing monkey

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the fallacy of composition
stories.head: Too many tomatoes spoil the price
body: When toma­toes are scarce, a farmer rea­sons that he should plant toma­toes, spend lav­ishly on in­puts and make a killing. For one farmer, that is sen­si­ble. {045-S05}

But a mil­lion farm­ers re­spond to the same prices. The mar­ket floods, the price falls to zero, and angry farm­ers pour truck­loads of toma­toes on the road­side be­cause they are not worth trans­port­ing.

Ajay Shah sees the same pat­tern in semi­con­duc­tors. After the chip short­age, he said, “every idiot in the world” de­cided to build a fab, and he pre­dicted a glut, and bank­rupt­cies among chip­mak­ers, within a year or two.
The dis­ci­plined ques­tion, he said, is al­ways the same: what hap­pens if ev­ery­body does this?

quote.text: What may be true for me in the small doesn’t work when a mil­lion peo­ple think the same.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the tomato glut

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why causes are hard to see
stories.head: Signal lost in the deep end
body: Does drop­ping a coin into water raise the level? In a lab­o­ra­tory, with a beaker and ev­ery­thing con­trolled, the ex­per­i­ment is easy. {045-S03}

“Now imag­ine you are doing this in a crowded swim­ming pool,” Amit Varma said. “It’s a big swim­ming pool, it is in­cred­i­bly crowded, peo­ple are splash­ing around in it, it is windy and it is rain­ing at the same time.” The data, he said, will mostly be garbage.
He had the metaphor from his friend Shruti Rajagopalan, who, he thinks, may have been quot­ing Don Boudreaux.

This is why econ­o­mists love the post-war splits of North and South Korea and East and West Germany: they come close to a con­trolled ex­per­i­ment on free mar­kets. “Spoiler alert,” Varma said: free mar­kets won.
stories.why: Social sci­ence hap­pens in the swim­ming pool, not the beaker. Real con­trolled ex­per­i­ments are rare, and con­fir­ma­tion bias fills the gap, so claims that X caused Y de­serve hu­mil­ity.

quiz.q: How many generations has modern man had, by Ajay Shah’s count, and why does it matter?

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 45. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Thomas Sowell, 1964 (public domain); Adam Smith, the Muir portrait (public domain); Friedrich Hayek (Mises Institute, CC BY-SA 3.0); Milton Friedman, Bachrach Studios, 1986 (public domain); a Chicago soup kitchen, February 1931 (US National Archives, public domain).

shelf.creator: Thomas Sowell
shelf.why: Sowell names foun­da­tional eco­nomic fal­la­cies from which many other er­rors grow; Amit says he fin­ished it a much clearer thinker about eco­nom­ics.

shelf.title: The Double ‘Thank You’ Moment
shelf.creator: John Stossel
shelf.why: Stossel’s sim­plest pic­ture of pos­i­tive-sum ex­change: when you buy a cof­fee, you thank the barista and the barista thanks you, be­cause both are bet­ter off.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: Profit = Philanthropy
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that in a world of vol­un­tary ex­change the only way to profit is by mak­ing some­one else bet­ter off, which makes profit an in­cen­tive to do good and the high­est form of phi­lan­thropy.

shelf.title: The Great Redistribution
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that mar­ket in­ter­ven­tions such as tar­iffs or bans on FDI in re­tail qui­etly move money from many dis­persed, poor con­sumers to a few or­gan­ised, rich in­ter­est groups, the op­po­site of their stated in­ten­tion.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Cooperation
shelf.creator: Robert Axelrod
shelf.why: Axelrod uses game the­ory to show why we evolved to co­op­er­ate, and for­malises the best re­sponse to being wronged: strike back once, but not for­ever, so some pun­ish­ment is op­ti­mal but grudges are not.

shelf.title: Tim Urban’s tweet on getting to know people
shelf.creator: Tim Urban
shelf.why: ‘Whenever I get to know some­one who seems per­fect, I end up dis­ap­pointed.

shelf.title: The Day Ryan Started Masturbating
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It is the full telling of the episode’s fun­ni­est il­lus­tra­tion of mis­tak­ing se­quence for cau­sa­tion.

shelf.title: ‘Wet streets cause rain’ (Michael Crichton on Gell-Mann Amnesia)
shelf.creator: Michael Crichton
shelf.why: Crichton’s ex­pla­na­tion of Gell-Mann Amnesia: we catch the media get­ting our own field wrong, then trust it on ev­ery­thing else.

shelf.title: The Forgotten Man
shelf.creator: Amity Shlaes
shelf.why: A con­trary his­tory of the Great Depression that Amit has a lot of sym­pa­thy for: gov­ern­ment in­ter­ven­tions, not the stock-market crash, turned a down­turn into a de­pres­sion.

shelf.title: Poker and Life (Episode 38)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: What Amit’s five years as a pro­fes­sional poker player taught him about life: most of what hap­pens is luck, so don’t let suc­cess go to your head or fail­ure crush you, and focus on doing the right things.

shelf.title: The Man of System (excerpted from The Theory of Moral Sentiments)
shelf.creator: Adam Smith
shelf.why: It is the clas­sic state­ment of the ar­ro­gance of imag­in­ing so­ci­ety as pieces on a chess­board that a plan­ner can move at will.

shelf.title: The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek names the core error be­hind cen­tral plan­ning and price con­trols: the be­lief that any­one can know enough to run a com­plex so­ci­ety from the top down, when the knowl­edge it needs is spread across ev­ery­one.

shelf.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s ar­gu­ment that the knowl­edge needed to run an econ­omy is dis­persed among mil­lions of peo­ple, and that prices, not plan­ners, carry it: a lan­guage through which strangers tell each other what they want and lack.

shelf.title: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts ex­plain land­mark pa­pers in plain lan­guage, no­tably Coase on why firms exist and Hayek on how prices co­or­di­nate a so­ci­ety no plan­ner can grasp.

shelf.title: What’s Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why Indian farm­ing, which em­ploys 40 to 60% of Indians against about 5% in rich coun­tries, is held back by the lack of a work­ing price sys­tem: MSPs that favour ce­re­als over pulses, loan waivers in­stead of struc­tural re­form, gluts and col­laps­ing prices.

shelf.title: The Selfish Gene
shelf.creator: Richard Dawkins
shelf.why: Dawkins’s metaphor of the self­ish gene which, read care­fully rather than lit­er­ally, ex­plains why hu­mans are ca­pa­ble of love and al­tru­ism.

shelf.title: Untitled
shelf.creator: Leonard Cohen
shelf.why: It is a slave speak­ing, say­ing that any sys­tem you de­sign with­out us will not work.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Understanding the State (Episode 25)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on mar­ket fail­ure in its pre­cise tech­ni­cal sense (pub­lic goods, ex­ter­nal­i­ties and the rest) and on the nar­row con­di­tions under which the state may in­ter­vene, con­di­tions that are nec­es­sary but not suf­fi­cient.

shelf.title: The Economics and Politics of Vaccines (Episode 223 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Ajay Shah)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Ajay on the eco­nom­ics and pol­i­tics of vac­cines, which Amit calls a pot­ted mas­ter­class on health­care: why pre­ven­tion beats cure, and why pub­lic health and health­care are dif­fer­ent things.

shelf.title: Declutter (Episode 30)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Much of the hosts’ per­sonal phi­los­o­phy of life: recog­nise your con­straints, es­pe­cially time, pri­ori­tise ac­cord­ingly, and pre­fer pro­cesses to grand goals.

shelf.title: Why We Fight: The Roots of War and the Paths to Peace
shelf.creator: Christopher Blattman
shelf.why: Ajay is glad an econ­o­mist has ‘opened the box of violence’.

shelf.title: The Three Languages of Politics
shelf.creator: Arnold Kling
shelf.why: A slim book you can read in an hour on why po­lit­i­cal dis­course is bro­ken: pro­gres­sives argue from equal­ity, con­ser­va­tives from tra­di­tion and lib­er­tar­i­ans from free­dom, so they talk past each other.

shelf.title: In My Tribe
shelf.creator: Arnold Kling
shelf.why: It con­tin­ues Kling’s think­ing, and Amit re­calls a fol­low-up there or else­where that adds nu­ance to the three-languages frame­work.

shelf.title: The Populist Playbook (Episode 42)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Populism is not ‘what is popular’ but a dan­ger­ous pack­age of be­liefs and meth­ods, ris­ing world­wide along­side na­tion­al­ism, that works by in­vent­ing en­e­mies and sell­ing in­su­lar slo­gans like im­port sub­sti­tu­tion.

laughs.text: The episode opens with both hosts fum­bling over who should speak first. Amit turns it into the the­sis: ‘both of us wanted the other one to go first, and we ended up kind of fight­ing over it. Not re­ally a fight, but it’s a good ques­tion. Why do we keep fight­ing?’
Amit scripts his own cue and Ajay obliges. Amit: ‘How does your first fal­lacy in­volve hunt­ing? I love it how you fol­low my in­struc­tions and ask me all the ques­tions I want.’

On catch­ing Ryan doing push-ups: ‘this goes against the eth­i­cal code... thin boys whose bones are vis­i­ble don’t do push-ups.’ After hear­ing the penance ex­pla­na­tion: ‘in my mind, I did sash­tang pranam and I just left.’
Six months later the girls are ‘gig­gling at the im­prob­a­ble pres­ence of a Greek god in their midst... and now I am the only per­son whose bones are vis­i­ble.’
Explaining cum hoc ergo propter hoc, Amit ad­mits: ‘I love the name be­cause of the main ac­tiv­ity in the story.’

On Ajay’s bis­cuit ex­per­i­ment: ‘I’m on keto diet, so if I press a but­ton, I don’t want a bis­cuit to come ever. Bacon strips, an­other mat­ter.’ He later re­veals his keto plus one-meal-a-day plan: ‘be­cause I want to be like Ryan. Which Ryan do I want to be like? Any of the two.’

Amit, on not gen­er­al­is­ing about econ­o­mists: ‘we know many econ­o­mists who are so­ciopaths, Ajay, I want to tell you that, but I know you’re not one of them. You’re a deeply emo­tional and em­pa­thetic per­son.’
Amit points to a graph and then cor­rects him­self: ‘when I say as you can see, I mean you, gen­tle reader. He can’t see any graph on the screen. There’s no screen, there’s only me.’
Amit, un­abashed: ‘I’m gonna be a lit­tle vain. I’m gonna name a law of eco­nom­ics after my­self be­cause I keep talk­ing about it and no one seems to get it.’

Ajay on in­vestor hubris: the dart-throwing mon­key beats nearly all stock pick­ers, ‘Of course, hope springs eter­nal. We each of us think that I’m in that 0.01% of the cool peo­ple that know what to do.’
Ajay teases Amit’s claim that India has learned to dis­trust top-down plan­ning: ‘Gentle read­ers, see how op­ti­mistic Amit is.’
‘PPP: per­pet­u­ally planned poverty’, a phrase coined by the hosts’ mu­tual friend Kumar Anand for what statism and zero-sum think­ing pro­duce.
‘Mai-baap sarkar kar degi’ (the par­ent-government will pro­vide). Amit says India’s ‘big­gest re­li­gion is government’, the mind­set that pow­ers the open-ended fal­lacy.
Adam Ferguson’s phrase that things hap­pen through ‘human ac­tion, but not human design’, in­voked with Hayek to de­scribe spon­ta­neous order.
Milton Friedman’s ‘no free lunch’, Ajay’s short­hand for the fact that gov­ern­ment money is nei­ther free nor in­fi­nite.
Robert Trivers’s work on al­tru­ism and self-interest, cited by Amit to argue that we are hard­wired for both, and that being al­tru­is­tic in­di­rectly serves our self-interest.

‘Pessimism of the in­tel­lect, op­ti­mism of the will’, the phrase Amit uses to an­swer the gloom: we see what is wrong but keep fight­ing. He fol­lowed it with ‘Everything is everything’ and then ad­mit­ted it ‘was a dra­matic way to end the chapter’.

entries.clue: Arnold, who hears politics spoken in three languages
He called the belief in top-down control the fatal conceit
When it is scarce, every farmer plants it
Amit’s diet: no biscuits, though bacon is another matter
Fallacy of the fan who stands up to see better
With its darts, it beats nearly every stock picker
Like the desires for health, safety and open space, in Sowell’s fallacy
The man of system moves people about like these
His Economic Facts and Fallacies set the episode’s agenda
After this, therefore because of this
Devout student whose penance was push-ups
Milton, who said there is no free lunch
It floods each spring, and the witch doctor’s coat takes the credit
